source.title: Evolutionary dynamics of cancer: From epigenetic regulation to cell population dynamics—mathematical model framework, applications, and open problems

accepted.question_text: Consider the non-delay one-dimensional epigenetic-state model on a state space Ω ⊂ R_+, where Q(t,x) is the density of resting-phase stem cells with epigenetic state x, c(t)=∫_Ω Q(t,x)ζ(x)dx is the effective cytokine concentration, β(c,x) is the proliferation rate, κ(x) is the differentiation/removal rate, μ(x) is the apoptosis rate during the proliferating phase, and p(x,y) is a normalized inheritance kernel satisfying ∫_Ω p(x,y)dx=1 for every y. For the steady state Q(t,x)=Q(x), determine whether there exists a positive scalar c such that the operator L_c[Q](x)=2∫_Ω β(c,y)e^{-μ(y)}p(x,y)Q(y)dy-(β(c,x)+κ(x))Q(x) has a nonnegative eigenfunction Q on Ω, and determine whether the resulting steady-state solution is unique and stable in the general case where p(x,y) depends on the mother-cell state y.
accepted.context_brief: Steady states for the nonlocal stem-cell regeneration equation

evidence.quote: Thus, the problem of the existence and uniqueness of the steady-state solution is reduced to a problem of finding a positive eigenvalue c of the operator Lc such that the corresponding eigenfunction Q(x) is non-negative for all x ∈ Ω.

For the transition probability p(x, y) independent of the state of the mother cell so that p(x, y) = p(x), the uniqueness and stability of the steady state were further discussed in [38]. However, open questions remain for general cases.

accepted.question_text: For the same non-delay model, let Q(t)=∫_Ω Q(t,x)dx be the total cell number, let f(t,x)=Q(t,x)/Q(t) be the fraction of cells with epigenetic state x, and define the multicellular entropy by E(t)=-∫_Ω f(t,x) log f(t,x)dx. Determine how to decompose the entropy derivative dE/dt into an entropy production rate epr and an entropy dissipation rate edr such that dE/dt=epr-edr and both epr and edr are always nonnegative, and characterize under what conditions the developmental dynamics described by the model—especially cancer development—produce increasing entropy.
accepted.context_brief: Entropy production and dissipation in heterogeneous cancer dynamics

evidence.quote: The entropy problem asks: how can we decompose the rate of entropy change into the entropy production rate (epr) and entropy dissipation rate (edr) such that dE/dt = epr − edr,

and both epr and edr are always non-negative? Solutions to this problem are essential to answer the question of how the entropy changes during the process of tissue development. In particular, is cancer development a process of increasing entropy [15, 42]?
For the general situation, it is not known how the entropy production rate and dissipation rate should be defined, and under which situation the development process leads to increasing entropy.

accepted.question_text: In the non-delay heterogeneous stem-cell regeneration model, the inheritance kernel p(x,y) is not directly measurable, while tumor burden Q(t) and the epigenetic-state distribution f(t,x)=Q(t,x)/Q(t) may be estimated from data such as imaging, liquid biopsies, biomarker measurements, and single-cell sequencing. Develop an inverse method that uses such observations to recover the rate functions β(c,x), κ(x), μ(x), and ζ(x), together with the transition kernel p(x,y), for a patient-specific model of cancer development.
accepted.context_brief: Parameter and kernel identification from experimental cancer data

evidence.quote: In the proposed model, the transition probability function p(x, y) is usually not known and cannot be measured directly from experiments. Hence, it is a challenging issue to estimate this transition function indirectly from experimental data.

Hence, the inverse problem of obtaining the rate functions β, κ, μ and ζ, and the transition function p(x, y), is essential for the development of personalized predictive models for cancer development.

accepted.question_text: Assume the epigenetic-state transition is local, so that p(x,y)=φ(y−x) with φ(r) supported only on |r|<ε≪1, normalized by ∫_{-∞}^{+∞}φ(r)dr=1, and having first two moments a=∫_{-∞}^{+∞}rφ(r)dr and D=∫_{-∞}^{+∞}r^2φ(r)dr. After expanding this local-transition kernel to second order and obtaining the closed-form evolution equation for the state distribution f(t,x), determine the corresponding steady states, entropy laws, and inverse problems in this local-transition regime; in particular, analyze the nonlinear eigenvalue problem for the steady-state parameter λ defined by the resulting second-order differential equation and its normalization constraints.
accepted.context_brief: Local-transition approximation of the epigenetic inheritance model

evidence.quote: In the equations (5.1) or (5.1)–(5.12), the epigenetic transition function p(x, y) is global. Here, we assume that the epigenetic state can have only local transitions, i.e., p(x, y) = φ(y − x)
From (5.23)–(5.25), the above questions of the steady state solution, the entropy problem, and the inverse problem can also be formulated as the problem of the local transition.
This equation defines a nonlinear eigenvalue problem for the eigenvalue λ.
